name: Freiwirtschaft
summary: Freiwirtschaft (free economy) is the market reform movement founded on Silvio Gesell's programme of Free-Land and Free-Money. It would put all land in public ownership and lease it by auction, with the rent paid to mothers by number of children, and it would charge holders of currency a carrying cost so money circulates and interest falls toward zero. Beyond that it keeps private enterprise, competition and free world trade, rejects Marxist nationalisation and centrally planned economies, and opposes tariffs, borders and nationalism.
scope: The classic Gesellian programme of Silvio Gesell's 'The Natural Economic Order' (Free-Land and Free-Money, 1916-1920), as described in the scholarship on the Free Economy movement (Preparata and Elliott 2004, Onken 2000) and the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland entry on the Freiwirtschaft movement. It covers the movement's core economic and land reform and its stated views on trade, borders and war. It excludes later revisions by followers, the movement's tactical dealings with the Nazi regime in 1933-34, and Keynes's critical discussion of Gesell. The preface's 1920s evolutionary and eugenic language is Gesell's own but is answered only where the statements ask about it.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Gesell calls his Natural Economic Order the 'Manchester System': once land and money privileges go, free competition without outside intervention does the allocating (Introduction).

public-ownership.rationale: Gesell rejects 'nationalisation or socialisation of production' as the communist answer; only land is taken into public hands and it is leased to private users (Introduction, Part II).

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In Weimar Gesell proposed a graduated wealth tax of up to 75 percent on large estates and big business to meet war costs, though it is a side proposal to his land and money reform.

unions-good.rationale: The sources record no position by Freiwirtschaft on this statement.

notes: Gesell's own text is the only full primary source; Keynes's chapter 23 was read but is a critic's and is not cited. Searched themes for more positions: government and democracy, women, religion, welfare and unions, taxation, immigration, war and colonies, trade, property and cooperatives. Gesell and his scholars say little on courts, policing, the environment, technology, speech, sexuality or religious law, so those stay null. The movement divided in 1924 between a moderate liberal Free Economy Federation and an anarchistic Physiocratic Task Force, which is why the state question is a split.
